 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
 PG-13 
 Action/Adventure , Drama , Sci-Fi/Fantasy 
 Content Caution
 Heavy Kids 
 Medium Tweens 
 Medium Teens 
 Light Adults 
 Credits
 In Theaters

 Runtime 
 2h 38m 
 Cast
 Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy; Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove; Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner and Merrilee Donner; Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow; Molly McCann as Louella McCoy; Iona Bell as Lou Lou; Percy Dagg IV as Ampert Latier; Jesse Plemons as Plutarch Heavensbee; Ralph Fiennes as President Snow; Maya Hawke as Wiress; Lili Taylor as Mags; Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee; Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket; Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle; Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman; Billy Porter as Magno Stift; Rada Rae as Wellie; Laura Marcus as Silka; Jhaleil Swaby as Panache; Woody Harrelson as Haymitch Abernathy (old); Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen; Josh Hutcherson as Peeta Mellark
 Home Release Date

 Director

 Distributor

 Reviewer
 Emily Tsiao 
 Parents' Guide Overview 
 On his 16 th birthday, Haymitch Abernathy is chosen as a tribute for the 50 th Annual Hunger Games—a brutal fight to the death against 47 other children. Sunrise on the Reaping may be the most hopeful film in the Hunger Games franchise, but it’s also possibly the most devastating. Horrific child deaths are the biggest cause for concern here, but the film also deals with heavier themes of alcoholism, torture and unjust actions for the supposed “greater good.”

 Conclusion 
 Movie Review
 It’s Reaping Day for the 50 th Annual Hunger Games. The Second Quarter Quell.
 It also happens to be Haymitch Abernathy’s birthday. He’s 16 years old today.
 If Haymitch is lucky, his name won’t get chosen. He won’t become a tribute for the Capitol to parade around. He won’t be sentenced to fight to the death in an arena with 47 other children.
 If it were up to Haymitch, the Hunger Games wouldn’t exist. The Capitol would not be in charge. President Snow would be deposed.
 Haymitch would like the sun to rise on his birthday without a Reaping …
 Unfortunately, the odds are not in Haymitch’s favor.
 When two boys and two girls are chosen from District 12—twice the normal number of tributes, in honor of the Quarter Quell—Haymitch’s name isn’t called. But the second boy selected doesn’t accept his fate: He tries to flee the Reaping. He gets shot. His mother rushes to his side. “Peacekeepers” try to drag her away. And then Lenore Dove Baird, the love of Haymitch’s decidedly young life, steps in.
 Peacekeepers threaten to kill Lenore Dove. So Haymitch steps in, too.
 For his defiance, Haymitch is selected to replace the boy who fled. Plutarch Heavensbee, the man filming the ceremony for the Capitol, resets the stage and gets the cameras rolling again. To the other districts in Panem, it now looks like Haymitch’s name was the one chosen all along.
 Haymitch boards a train for the Capitol. For several days, Capitol citizens will gawk and leer at Haymitch and his fellows. They’ll assess the skills of the tributes and bet on the winner during the televised event. They’ll send helpful gifts to their favorites. They’ll return to their gaudy, eccentric and overly indulgent lifestyles the moment the Games end.
 And next year, on Haymitch’s birthday—when Haymitch will likely be dead—they’ll do it all again.
 But what if it didn’t have to be that way? What if the Hunger Games weren’t inevitable? What if Haymitch’s own death wasn’t a guarantee?
 What might happen if a few brave individuals stood against Snow and the Capitol and said enough was enough? And what if they managed to get their quiet rebellion televised during the Games? 
 Well, that sort of resistance just might spark a hope in Panem that hasn’t been seen in 50 years. It may even catch fire.
 Positive Elements
 Haymitch is a veritable paragon of goodness. At home, he helps out his mother and takes care of his little brother—both of whom he loves very much. Around his district, he’s helpful and kind. He’s not beloved , per se, but he is respected and generally well-liked.
 Haymitch takes that goodhearted spirit with him to the Capitol. He doesn’t necessarily want to die in the Games, but he doesn’t want to watch anyone else die either. So he determines to help his fellow tributes, particularly his friends from District 12, keeping them out of harm’s way and sharing his very limited resources. He even agrees to help a small band of rebels shut down the Games from inside the arena—which they hope will end the Hunger Games for good—risking his own life to do so.
 Most of the tributes don’t want the Games to turn them into savages in order to survive. One girl says she doesn’t want to lose her dignity, so she won’t beg for her life. She kindly fashions necklaces to hold the tokens of the other tributes (the only item from home that they’re allowed to take into the arena). Inside the arena, she crafts a fork and spoon for herself, so she won’t have to eat what little food exists with her bare hands.
 Another tribute hopes he can simply live well with what little time he has left. He comes from a family of bookmakers (people who arrange bets for the Games)—which is very much taboo in the districts, given the fact that the tributes hail from those districts—but he wants to prove that he’s not like them. Yes, he can rattle off the odds of survival for the other tributes, but he doesn’t want that to be his legacy. He wants to be known as someone who helped his friends beat the odds.
 Before the Reaping, a teenage girl cries, scared for what’s to come. But she says she’ll stop crying before the ceremony because she won’t allow the Capitol to use her tears for their entertainment.
 Throughout the Hunger Games, we see several young tributes sacrifice themselves to protect their friends. We learn that a man leading a rebellion against the Capitol took full blame for the incident when caught: He never gave up the names of his fellow conspirators.
 A few Capitol citizens step up to assist the neglected District 12 tributes prepare for their public debut and other ceremonies that precede the Games. Those same people are kind to the tributes, offering them words of hope. Haymitch’s friends and girlfriend back home are ever encouraging.
 Many people, including a couple of Capitol citizens, suggest that Snow could be overthrown if the districts simply stop submitting to the Capitol. District citizens greatly outnumber Capitol citizens, and they also provide the majority of the Capitol’s resources. These people choose to be brave and risk their lives to stand up to Peacekeepers and Snow, hoping that their courage will inspire hope in others.
 Spiritual Elements
 We hear just a little talk about fate: Many people believe the Hunger Games are “inevitable,” but others believe it’s possible to change that. A funeral song mentions heaven.
 Lenore Dove tells Haymitch that she doesn’t believe people disappear entirely when they die: She thinks they simply move from one “place” to another. Haymitch adopts this line of thinking and shares it with his friends in the arena. He says that his mother had twin daughters who died after being born prematurely, and he believes that they are still together, wherever they are.
 The Capitol has made a science of breeding “mutts,” genetically enhanced and mutated animals that are completely under the control of the Gamemakers (the people who control the Hunger Games).
 Sexual & Romantic Content
 Haymitch and Lenore Dove cozy up to each other whenever they’re together, holding hands and sharing some affectionate kisses.
 Several young women wear outfits that display cleavage or midriffs. A troupe of female dancers wear leotards while they perform, showing lots of leg and cleavage. We see several male tributes with their shirts off, and one boy rips off his shirt during an interview to show off his muscular frame.
 Several teen boys (with towels wrapped around their waists) are hosed down. We see Haymitch from the belly up on a couple of occasions as he showers or bathes. Capitol stylists primp the tributes before some televised ceremonies, and they discuss the removal of body hair. One woman, equipped with a razor, tells Haymitch she’ll be “down there” before dipping below camera, apparently to shave his nether regions.
 When a female tribute threatens one of the girls from District 12, the girl sarcastically bites back, “You flirting with me?” When a snake slithers onto a man’s shoulder, he jokes, “I haven’t been touched like this in years.”
 We see a man in some boxer shorts and a tank top. One teen girl wears a spaghetti-strap top, though it’s unclear if this is a bra or a camisole.
 Violent Content
 The body count here totals out at 51 dead kids, plus two adults. There could be more, certainly, but those are the ones we can confirm. We don’t see each of these deaths onscreen—and the ones we do see are not particularly bloody or gory—though that doesn’t change the devastating effect.
 The first child to die is the boy from District 12 who didn’t want to be reaped. He gets shot in the back, and when his mother rushes to his side, armed Peacekeepers try to drag her away. Lenore Dove steps in only to get pushed around herself. And when Haymitch tries to intervene, he receives the butt of a gun to the forehead, leaving a sizeable bruise.
 The next death occurs before the Games even begin. During a parade, Capitol citizens throw colorful smoke grenades at the procession of tributes. The horses pulling the tributes get spooked and begin charging, chariots and all, through the crowd. Several chariots crash, and when two chariots collide, a young girl gets trapped beneath one and dragged for several yards. Her skin is covered in road rash, and she expires shortly after. (We later learn that the man responsible for the parade was poisoned for his failure to control the stampede.)
 An additional 47 children die during the course of the Games themselves. Roughly half are killed during the initial skirmish, when all the kids rush to the center of the arena to collect weapons and supplies. Once armed, they begin slicing and dicing their way through the other tributes. Some are stabbed or shot with arrows. One boy takes a hatchet to the back. Those who survive are covered in cuts and bruises.
 Mutts (purposefully mutated animals controlled by the Gamemakers) attack the tributes, too. One boy is beset by butterflies that try to electrocute him. Another gets swarmed by squirrels that bite him and tear at his flesh, eventually killing him. Two kids get covered in leech-like berries. And one girl falls victim to a flock of birds that peck at her. She dies because one of the birds manages to puncture her windpipe.
 More children die when the Gamemakers trigger a volcano. Haymitch flees the resulting inferno and gets blasted off his feet. (He only survives because the Capitol-provided uniforms are fireproof.) Other environmental traps include poisonous plants and water. One young girl, after inhaling the pollen of some pretty flowers, suffocates, her nose bleeding from the noxious dust. A rabbit begins bleeding from the eyes and dies after drinking toxic water. Haymitch nearly suffers the same fate, but he’s able to administer an antidote of charcoal to himself before the toxins take effect.
 Though he tries to avoid fighting, Haymitch kills at least two other tributes in self-defense. One of his friends kills a large boy with a poisonous dart. One girl is killed by her own blade when it ricochets off a forcefield back into her chest.
 A woman and her child burn to death when Capitol agents seal their home and set fire to the structure. We don’t see the victims, but we do see the blazing house. Their bodies are buried in a single coffin, we’re told, because they were found holding each other in their arms, and those handling the burial thought it was right to keep them together.
 When a teenager accidentally ingests a poisoned treat, she tries to induce vomiting by putting her fingers down her throat. But it’s no use: Because she lives in a poor district, she hasn’t eaten in several days, and there’s simply nothing in her stomach to throw up. She perishes shortly after, gasping for breath.
 Haymitch wanders outside the boundaries of the arena, hoping that the Gamemakers will track him and kill him there. His reasoning is that if he dies outside the arena, everyone will know he died on his own terms, rather than the Capitol’s.
 Many, many fights take place in the arena. During one scuffle, two teens barely able to stand (due to previous injuries) face off against each other, adding to each other’s injuries before one of them is killed. One girl’s eye is swollen shut by a grisly cut. Haymitch’s ear bleeds badly after it gets nicked by a thrown hatchet. A friend stitches a deep cut on Haymitch’s torso after a battle, and he’s asked to display the wound to Capitol citizens later on.
 One teenage boy tackles another in anger, starting a fight between the tributes. Everyone picks up weapons and prepares to defend themselves, but Peacekeepers intervene. When the teens are told to put the weapons down and place their hands on their heads, they comply. However, one girl later points out that they could have resisted the Peacekeepers, who were unarmed.
 Several conspirators are tortured for information. We don’t see this occur onscreen, but one man wakes from his experience drooling and connected to what is presumably a machine designed to induce pain. Two other victims show up later, covered in bruises. (Though not explained or depicted here, we learn that one of the victims suffered a stroke during her torture, permanently impeding her speech. The other endured such severe psychological trauma that she developed physical tics and speech difficulties.)
 Peacekeepers are anything but. They use force without qualm, often firing their weapons into the air to induce fear. And they have no problem manhandling women and children. We’re told the Capitol controls the districts through hangings, shootings and simply starving the citizens.
 Someone uses a makeshift explosive to blow up a water tank. The flood of water takes down some Peacekeepers, and it’s unclear whether they drown.
 Elsewhere, another explosive is used to take out a force field and a hovercraft. The person who triggered the explosion is badly injured, but he survives. When he limps onto a stage after recovering, someone mocks his gait.
 A woman slaps a teenage girl after the girl insults her. The girl initially slaps her back, warning the woman not to touch her again. But the woman simply picks up what looks like a riding crop and beats the girl mercilessly, leaving welts all over the girl’s arms. She only stops when she’s reminded that the girl has to appear on television the next day and cannot show signs of abuse.
 We’re told that one victor never had to lay a hand on a fellow tribute: She won the Games by manipulating the arena to her favor.
 A past victor is forced to mentor his own son in the Hunger Games. He says that he tried to rebel against the Capitol, so they reaped his son to punish him. He seems convinced that his son will not survive the Games, so he asks Haymitch to make sure that the boy at least doesn’t suffer. When the Games are over, we’re told the man won’t kill himself because it would dishonor his son’s memory.
 We learn that when a man administers poison to his enemies, he ingests the stuff himself to disguise his guilt, simply taking an antidote before the poison can kill him. A man cuts his hand on a glass cup when he crushes it in anger. (He licks the blood off his fingers.)
 Career tributes (kids who are trained to compete in the Games from a young age) arrive at the Capitol in handcuffs, owing to their propensity for violence. A guy shoves around his friends and throws some empty bottles at them to scare them off.
 Someone wears tiny live snakes as earrings. He’s told the earrings have been banned, but he brushes it off, saying the snakes will be dead in an hour anyway. After the volcanic eruption, Haymitch finds a badly burnt fox gasping for air.
 Crude or Profane Language
 Single uses of “a–” and “p-ss.”
 Drug & Alcohol Content
 Haymitch doesn’t drink. He’s offered alcoholic beverages on several occasions, but he always declines. When someone from District 12 pays him with a bottle of booze, he sells it to a medicinal shop, calling it “cough syrup” since alcohol is illegal in the districts. The shopkeeper tells him that many people will be looking for such a “remedy” on Reaping Day.
 However, after Haymitch survives the games and watches so many of his loved ones die at the hands of the Capitol, he decides to imbibe. He consumes more and more of the stuff to numb his emotional pain, eventually becoming the alcoholic that we know from other films in the series.
 A Capitol woman smokes cigarettes and drinks alcohol whenever she’s not presenting on camera. We’re told that the Capitol sometimes drugs people to control them.
 Other Noteworthy Elements
 President Snow is manipulative and cunning. He doesn’t just control the events of the Hunger Games, he controls the tributes, too. Rebels plot against him, but unsuccessfully. He orders many people to be either killed or tortured. And he truly believes that the Hunger Games, the merciless murder of children, are the best insurance against future rebellion.
 When a tribute accidentally dies before the Hunger Games begin, the Capitol replaces her with a lookalike. Haymitch and his friends are told that the new girl was likely the child of rebels, kidnapped, drugged and tortured by the Capitol. Indeed, the girl acts quite robotic, repeating the same phrase over and over, wandering into danger without heed and woefully unaware of her surroundings.
 Most Capitol citizens do not consider the Hunger Games to be evil. For them, it’s sheer entertainment. In fact, they believe there is glory to be found in winning the Games. But more than that, they’ve been fed the lie that this is an appropriate punishment for the district rebellion (and civil war) that occurred 50 years ago.
 As such, those who run the Games do everything in their power to maintain that propaganda. If someone acts out of order on camera, they’ll reset and reshoot the scene. Peacekeepers are criticized when they kill someone onscreen, though a time-delayed broadcast allows them to cut that part out of the footage. Failure to put on a good show can result in a person’s death—and the murder of their family. When Plutarch advises a reshoot that prevents a girl’s death, Haymitch thanks him for saving her life. But Plutarch says he didn’t do it to save her life: He did it because it’s his job to create the best show possible.
 Drusilla, District 12’s tribute escort, is an ostentatious woman with obvious signs of cosmetic surgery to make herself look younger. (Someone jokes that she’s been serving the Capitol for 2,500 years.) She wears outfits that restrict her movement, and she even has to be carted onto the stage on Reaping Day since she can’t walk properly—and all due to personal vanity.
 Because the Reaping ceremony didn’t go as planned, Drusilla forbids the tributes from saying goodbye to their families. Haymitch is the exception since Plutarch insists he needs the “tearful goodbye” footage.
 Many in the Capitol, including Drusilla, consider District 12 beneath them. (Though Drusilla has no problem taking credit for the tributes’ success.) A stylist tasked with dressing 12’s tributes ignores his duties. He shows up to ceremonies at the last minute having put zero effort into their wardrobes. In one instance, rather than clothing them, he simply drapes a large snake on one girl’s shoulders over her paper hospital-like gown.
 Once they’re in the Capitol, the tributes are assigned mentors—usually the previous victors from their districts. However, District 12 has only ever had one victor, and she disappeared shortly after surviving the Games. As such, the 12s “borrow” mentors from other districts.
 It’s strongly implied that many who live in District 12 are starving due to the Capitol’s neglect. They are essentially kept prisoner there with an electric fence along the border (though it doesn’t always work). Many people only manage to survive by going outside this fence to search for food and other needed resources.
 Some of the victors of past Hunger Games show signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. More than a few Capitol citizens berate and belittle the tributes, even suggesting that they deserve to die.
 Many verbal insults are exchanged. Maysilee, one of the District 12 tributes, can be quite rude to people she thinks are uncouth. While searching for allies, the son of a bookmaker rattles off the odds of survival to other tributes—and Haymitch warns him that doing so might scare them off. A teen girl gets arrested for singing songs that are considered illegal.
 People lie. Haymitch blames himself for the deaths of his friends because he was unable to save them. In the years to come, as a victor and mentor, he seems to blame himself for the deaths of the tributes from his district since he is helpless to save them either.
 [ Spoiler warning ] When the Games end and Haymitch is crowned the victor, he learns the Capitol edited footage to make him look like a traitor to his friends and allies. All of his heroic actions are painted to look like selfish survivalist behavior. A TV personality says that Haymitch’s “negligence, not knife” killed his friends. And the Capitol labels him as its “definitive poster child,” saying it was his “savage cunning,” not heroism, that won him the Games.
 Conclusion
 Sunrise on the Reaping feels like simultaneously the most devasting Hunger Games film and the most hopeful.
 If you’re planning to see this film, be prepared to watch a lot of kids die. Be prepared to watch a teenage boy blame himself for those deaths, even though there’s nothing he could have done to stop them. Be prepared to watch him dive into a life of debauchery—an attempt to numb the pain he feels year after year as he watches even more kids enter the Hunger Games arenas to be killed.
 But also, be prepared to leave the film with a sense of victory.
 Winning the Hunger Games is not a victory, which Haymitch well knows. However, joining the rebellion that eventually ends the Games for good is a victory.
 Haymitch drowns himself in booze after he leaves the arena because he doesn’t know when the Capitol will finally be overthrown. It could be generations, he’s told, before enough people have the courage to fight back.
 But in the meantime, if people like Haymitch are willing to keep the fight going—if they’re willing to endure torture and abuse, year after year—then that small spark of hope will never die. As long as there’s someone around to continue fanning the flame of resistance, change will eventually come.
 And Haymitch is willing to be that fan for as long as it takes.
 In addition to the brutality at work here, there’s a small amount of language and questionable costume choices to navigate. The denizens of the Capitol are a piece of work, lauding the Games as a wonderful and entertaining event that keep the “selfish” districts in line. The people who run the Games are worse, verbally and physically abusing the tributes before they even make it into the arena.
 All of those elements take this film well out of the range for younger viewers. Even teens may be hard-pressed to navigate this film on their own.
 But if your family does decide to watch Sunrise on the Reaping , be sure to discuss the themes at play. Talk about why it’s important to think through our entertainment choices—lest we become complacent like the Capitol’s citizenry. Ask yourselves whether consuming films like this desensitizes us to violent content. Talk about ways we can stand up to evil without resorting to cruelty ourselves.
 And perhaps even lean on the Word of God: John 15:13 says, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” In Sunrise , Haymitch proves that he’s willing to do whatever it takes to protect his allies and stop the Hunger Games for good. And that’s a positive attribute worth talking about.
 Back to Top 
 Emily Tsiao
 Emily studied film and writing when she was in college. And when she isn’t being way too competitive while playing board games, she enjoys food, sleep, and geeking out with her husband indulging in their “nerdoms,” which is the collective fan cultures of everything they love, such as Star Wars, Star Trek, Stargate and Lord of the Rings.
